lesson.title: Why Color Blindness Runs in Sons: X-Linked Inheritance
lesson.summary: Tracking X-linked alleles through a Punnett square, using red green color blindness as the working example, shows precisely why X-linked recessive conditions turn up so much more often in males.
lesson.body:
Because an X-linked gene lives on the X chromosome, its alleles are usually written as superscripts attached to the X itself, and a male's genotype is written with his Y chromosome shown explicitly, since he carries only one X. Let X-B represent the dominant allele for normal color vision and X-b represent the recessive allele associated with red green color blindness.

Work through a cross between a carrier mother, genotype X-B X-b, who has normal vision herself but carries one copy of the recessive allele, and an unaffected father, genotype X-B Y. The mother produces X-B and X-b gametes in equal proportion. The father produces X-B and Y gametes in equal proportion. Combining them in a Punnett square gives four equally likely offspring genotypes: X-B X-B, X-B X-b, X-B Y, and X-b Y.

Sorting those four outcomes by sex is the key step. Daughters always receive the father's X chromosome plus one of the mother's two X chromosomes, so a daughter is either X-B X-B, with normal vision, or X-B X-b, a carrier with normal vision, since she always receives a normal X-B from her father to pair with whatever she got from her mother. Sons always receive the father's Y chromosome plus one of the mother's two X chromosomes, so a son is either X-B Y, with normal vision, or X-b Y, colorblind, with a one half chance of being affected, because he has only the single X he inherited from his mother and nothing from his father to cover for it.

That asymmetry, sons at real risk from a carrier mother while none of that same cross's daughters are ever affected, is the signature pattern of X-linked recessive inheritance, and it follows directly from hemizygosity. Red green color blindness and hemophilia are both real human conditions inherited this way. The reverse cross is informative too: an affected father, X-b Y, crossed with a homozygous unaffected mother, X-B X-B, produces daughters who are all carriers, X-B X-b, and sons who are all unaffected, X-B Y, since a son never inherits his father's X chromosome at all.
